title: How do you build business judgement if you are new to business?
description: Consultants connect numbers to business decisions. You want to recognise familiar patterns, not copy an executive’s personality or body language.
hook: You build business judgement by asking the same three questions of every business story you meet (how does it make money, what drives its profit, and what would you recommend) and by learning one business idea a day well enough to explain it aloud. If you do not come from a business background, case language can feel foreign at first. Fifteen to twenty minutes a day of the right kind of reading and watching changes that quickly.
body:
What business judgement means in a case

In a case, judgement is the ability to connect numbers to decisions. It shows up when you spot that a 2% price rise would close a cost gap, when you notice that a $100k profit forecast needs an unrealistic number of customers, or when you suggest the one analysis that would change the client's mind. It is not about knowing every industry or sounding like an executive. It is about recognising common patterns: how revenue is built, where costs sit, and what usually goes wrong.

The fastest way in is to understand how businesses make money, then practise applying that to real companies every day.

Three exercises for 15 to 20 minutes a day

1. Watch or read one business story, with three questions

Pick a founder interview, a CEO podcast, an episode of Shark Tank or one business news article. Pause and ask:

  • What is the business model, and who pays?
  • What drives profit: price, volume, or costs?
  • What would I recommend, and what would I want to check first?

You can also notice how good speakers explain things: a measured pace, simple words, pauses. Borrow the techniques, but keep your own style. For where to find good material, see business news and podcasts worth your time.

2. Learn one business idea

Take one concept a day and learn it properly: what it means, how it is calculated, and when it matters in a case. Good starting points are unit economics, customer acquisition cost, churn, contribution margin, pricing power, switching costs and operating leverage.

3. Explain it in your own words

Give a 60-second explanation of today's idea using a real or invented company, out loud. Then write one useful phrase in a vocabulary note. If you cannot explain it simply, you have not learned it yet.

Turn a headline into a hypothesis

Reading the news passively builds vocabulary but not much judgement. The habit that builds judgement is converting a headline into a driver, an economic mechanism and an assumption you could test.

Suppose you read that a retailer is opening smaller stores. Instead of memorising what management did, ask why smaller stores might do better: lower rent, being closer to customers, fewer staff, faster shopping, or a range tailored to the neighbourhood. Then challenge each reason. Smaller stores can mean higher delivery cost per item and less shelf space, so fewer products to sell. Now you have a view and a list of things to check, which is what a hypothesis is.

A worked example: does this store make sense?

A new store needs $500k of investment and is forecast to make $100k of operating profit a year. That is a simple payback of $500k ÷ $100k = 5 years, before tax and ignoring how cash flows change over time.

Judgement means asking whether the $100k is plausible. Build it up with illustrative assumptions:

  • Revenue of $1M a year at a 30% gross margin gives $300k of gross profit.
  • Rent of $120k and staff costs of $80k leave $300k − $120k − $80k = $100k.
  • $1M of revenue at an average basket of $20 needs $1M ÷ $20 = 50,000 transactions a year, about 137 a day if the store opens every day.

Now the forecast has testable parts. Is 137 customers a day realistic for this location? Is $120k of rent right for the size? If footfall turns out to be 100 a day, revenue falls to about $730k, gross profit to about $219k, and operating profit to about $19k, stretching the payback past 25 years. That sensitivity is the insight.

What judgement sounds like

Weak:

The store makes $100k a year, so it pays back in five years, which seems fine.

Strong:

Payback is five years, but the profit is very sensitive to footfall. We need about 137 customers a day; at 100, profit almost disappears. I'd want to check footfall at similar stores before committing.

The strong answer does the same maths and then asks what would have to be true.

Common mistakes

  • Collecting facts instead of patterns. Knowing a company's revenue matters less than knowing why its margin is high or low.
  • Copying an executive's personality. Judgement is in the reasoning, not the tone.
  • Looking only at revenue. Always ask what it costs to earn that revenue.
  • Long, rare sessions. Fifteen minutes most days beats a weekend binge.

Try it now

1. A subscription meal-kit company says it will double marketing spend to grow faster. What would you want to know first?

Show the answer

Whether each new customer is profitable: how much it costs to acquire one, how much profit they bring per month, and how long they stay before cancelling. If customers churn before repaying their acquisition cost, doubling marketing doubles the losses.

2. Explain operating leverage in 60 seconds using a cinema as the example.

Show the answer

"A cinema's costs are mostly fixed: rent, staff and film deals don't change much with the number of tickets sold. So once it covers those costs, almost every extra ticket is profit, and a small rise in attendance lifts profit sharply. The flip side is that a small fall hurts just as much. That is operating leverage."

3. In the store example, what daily footfall would you need for a three-year payback?

Show the answer

Three-year payback on $500k needs about $167k of profit a year. Add back $200k of rent and staff to get $367k of gross profit, so revenue of $367k ÷ 30% ≈ $1.22M. At $20 a basket that is about 61,000 transactions, or roughly 167 a day.

Where to practise next

If you are switching from another field, read preparing without a business background. The interview skills page collects this routine alongside the thinking and speaking exercises.
